archetype.name: Pocket Passer (timing and accuracy)
archetype.definition: Burrow wins from the pocket with fast, accurate throws into the intermediate windows. He rarely runs and avoids sacks by getting the ball out, and this year he is distributing it more conservatively than he did in his best seasons.

report.headline: Elite intermediate throwing is masking a short game that keeps bleeding points
report.take:
Burrow is the same quarterback he has been for years: a quick, accurate pocket thrower who rarely beats himself with bad throws and lives at the second level of the defense. His 7.6% bad-throw rate ranks 6th of 32 charted passers, his CPOE of +4.6 sits right where it was in 2025, and his 2.57-second time to throw is in line with his career band of 2.54 to 2.80. The Bengals lean on him harder than any team leans on its quarterback. Their +7.2% pass rate over expected ranks 1st, and that is why he is 4th in passing yards while only 19th in EPA per dropback.

The season is split almost in half by depth. Throws 10-19 yards downfield have been absurd: +0.98 EPA per attempt, a 76% success rate and a +19.3 CPOE on 42 attempts. The 12 deep shots added three touchdowns and +1.69 per attempt. Everything at or near the line has gone the other way. The 27 throws behind the line produced -0.32 per play, and the 76 short throws produced -0.24 per play along with all three interceptions. Chase Brown has drawn 24 targets at -0.27 EPA each. The offense has been efficient whenever Burrow pushes the ball and inefficient whenever it plays safe, and it has played safe a lot: his 12.7% aggressiveness is the lowest of any season here except 2023.

The totals hide a few things. His 0.114 EPA per dropback undersells how well he has thrown since Week 2. Game passing EPA went -2.6, -0.5, +14.7 and +7.4, and the Houston game (five sacks, 19.4% bad throws) is the only truly poor outing. In the other direction, the 428-yard Week 4 came on 54 attempts while trailing Jacksonville, so the yardage average is padded by volume rather than efficiency. His game-state splits are backward from what you'd expect. He has been excellent trailing by 9+ (+0.44 EPA) and poor leading by 9+ (-0.27), which suggests the offense turns conservative with a lead.

Going forward, the short-game drag looks more like noise than a skill change. A 68% completion rate on short throws should not produce -0.24 per play, and three interceptions on 76 attempts is mostly what is sinking it. The intermediate numbers will cool, but they rest on a real, career-long strength. The bigger near-term variable is his receivers. Tee Higgins (groin) and Ja'Marr Chase (concussion) are both questionable, and they account for 67 of his targets at better than +0.56 EPA each.

strengths.title: Owns the intermediate middle tier
strengths.body: Throws of 10-19 air yards have been the engine of the offense, with a success rate near three in four and completions far above expectation. That comes from his timing and ball placement against zone, and it is the same profile that produced his 2021 and 2024 seasons. A +19 CPOE will not hold over a full season, but this is a real skill, not a hot streak.

strengths.title: Clean throws, few sacks taken
strengths.body: His bad-throw rate ranks 6th and his 25.9% pressure-to-sack rate is the best of his career, which had never been below 29.4%. Quick processing, rather than a clean pocket, is turning pressure into throwaways and completions. The accuracy is a career constant. The sack avoidance is newer, so expect it to settle somewhat.

strengths.title: Volume baked into the scheme
strengths.body: No offense passes more over expectation, and the run game sits 18th in EPA, so the ball is going to stay in his hands. That keeps his yardage and fantasy floor high even in games where efficiency dips.

concerns.title: Short game and check-downs are leaking
concerns.body: Throws behind the line and under 10 yards make up 103 of his 157 attempts, and both are deeply negative in EPA. The three interceptions are concentrated there, and the running-back target share is producing negative value. Part of this is likely variance on the picks, since the completion rate is fine. But a low-aggressiveness approach that leans on these throws caps how efficient the offense can be.

concerns.title: Offense goes conservative with a lead
concerns.body: With a 9+ point lead his EPA turns sharply negative, and close fourth quarters have also been below water. A smaller sample of trailing snaps shows the opposite. The pattern fits a lower-risk plan once ahead, and it matters this week because Cincinnati is a 7-point favorite.

concerns.title: Top two receivers both questionable
concerns.body: Higgins and Chase are his two most-targeted and among his most efficient receivers. Chase left Week 4 with a concussion, and Higgins is day-to-day with an adductor injury. Burrow is also hit or sacked on 19.3% of dropbacks behind a line whose hit rate ranks 28th, so a thinner receiving corps that holds the ball longer would raise that risk.

trend.note: Game passing EPA climbed from -2.6 and -0.5 in the first two weeks to +14.7 at Pittsburgh and +7.4 against Jacksonville. The losses in Weeks 3 and 4 came despite his play, not because of it.

nextGame.headline: Bottom-tier Miami pass defense, but receiver health and script loom
nextGame.body:
Miami's defense is built opposite to how Burrow wins. It ranks 29th in pass EPA allowed and 9th against the run, generates almost no sacks (28th in sack rate) and is 29th defending short throws. That is exactly the area where Cincinnati has been failing, so this is a chance to fix the weak part of his game. The defense allows 17.4 PPR points and two touchdowns a game to quarterbacks, middle-of-the-pack figures that likely reflect opponents running out leads against a struggling offense. Miami's offense is 29th in EPA and 31st in success rate, and it is now without De'Von Achane (IR) and WR Caleb Douglas.

On Miami's side, edge rusher Robert Beal Jr. is out and safety Dante Trader Jr. (73% of snaps) is questionable. Losing Trader would weaken the deep middle, where Burrow's intermediate throws live. The cornerbacks listed as out, Reese Taylor and Storm Duck, haven't played this year, so they change nothing. On his side, everything hinges on Higgins and Chase. With both healthy this looks like a big efficiency spot. If one or both sit, the targets shift toward Gesicki, Dohnte Meyers and Chase Brown, and Brown's targets have been unproductive. Burrow's own early-season questionable tag is stale: he took 100% of snaps in all four games.

keyMatchups.title: Burrow vs a soft, pass-rush-light defense
keyMatchups.body: Miami ranks near the bottom in both pass EPA allowed and sack rate. A clean pocket should let Burrow work the intermediate zone at will, and the defense's weakness on short throws should make his check-downs productive again.

keyMatchups.title: Higgins and Chase availability
keyMatchups.body: These two have combined for 67 targets at well over +0.5 EPA per target. If both are out, Gesicki (+1.0 per target on 15) is the most efficient fallback. The rest of the depth chart has been far less productive.

keyMatchups.title: Lead-protecting game script
keyMatchups.body: Miami's offense rarely sustains drives and runs far below league pass rates. Cincinnati could therefore build a lead early and lean on the run, which is the game state where Burrow has struggled. A big lead caps his volume even if his efficiency is strong.

nextGame.watch: Whether Higgins and Chase are active, and whether Cincinnati keeps pushing the ball downfield after taking a two-score lead.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect his efficiency to rise from its current 19th-place EPA toward his usual range of roughly 0.15 to 0.20 per play. The short-pass interceptions and the Week 1-2 struggles weigh on the total, and both look more like variance than decline: his accuracy, sack avoidance and CPOE all match his good seasons. The intermediate and deep numbers will come down, since a +19 CPOE and three touchdowns on 12 deep attempts aren't sustainable. That makes the net picture solid but less spectacular than the last two games.

Volume is the stable part. A league-high pass rate over expected and a below-average run game keep him around 35-40 attempts a game, and that supports a high yardage floor. The main risks are receiver health, with both top receivers currently banged up, and a line that lets him get hit often. Those two together could turn small efficiency dips into turnover-heavy games.

bets.reason: Miami is 29th in pass EPA allowed and 28th in sack rate. Burrow has four red-zone touchdowns on 16 attempts and three deep scores, and in a 7-point favorite's script the points are likely to come through the air early.

The average is inflated by a 428-yard, 54-attempt game played from behind. As a 7-point favorite against an offense ranked 31st in success rate, Cincinnati should be protecting a lead, where Burrow's EPA turns negative. Both top receivers are also questionable, and Miami allows just 244.8 yards a game to quarterbacks.

Miami's offense is 29th in EPA, runs far more than expected and has lost Achane and Douglas. Cincinnati's defense ranks 10th in EPA and 2nd in sack rate, so Miami may not hold up its end of a 43-point game.

confidence.note: Four games of data, with big depth splits on small samples and both top receivers questionable.
